beats.content: The Spring Boot DIP pattern is three steps. Define an interface like UserRepository. Annotate the concrete class with @Repository. Inject the interface in the high-level class via constructor. Spring handles the wiring.

The key habit is always injecting the interface type, not the concrete class type. @Autowired UserRepository is correct. @Autowired JpaUserRepository is a DIP violation because you're depending on the concrete class directly.

sharp edge: when Spring finds two classes implementing the same interface, it throws a NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException. You fix this with @Primary on one implementation or @Qualifier on the injection point. Knowing this shows you've actually used DIP with Spring in practice.

sections.title: How Spring Boot Enables DIP
sections.content:
Spring Boot's **IoC (Inversion of Control) container** is built to enforce DIP automatically. You define an interface representing what your high-level class needs—like **UserRepository** or **PaymentGateway**.

You annotate concrete implementations with **@Repository**, **@Service**, or **@Component**. In your high-level class, you inject the **interface type**, not the concrete class. Spring scans for classes that implement that interface, creates instances, and injects them at runtime. Your service class never calls new on the implementation—it doesn't even know which implementation exists. This is DIP in action: the service depends on the abstraction, Spring provides the implementation. If you add a second implementation, Spring can choose which one based on **@Primary** or **@Qualifier**. The high-level module's code doesn't change. This is the power of combining DIP with Spring's IoC—you get decoupling with almost zero boilerplate.

sections.title: Spring Boot DIP Example with Interfaces
When to Apply DIP with Spring
sections.content:
Use Spring's DIP support for **infrastructure dependencies**: repositories, external API clients, message queues, email services, caching layers. These are components that have multiple possible implementations or that you need to mock in tests.

Apply it when you have **cross-cutting concerns** managed by Spring: transaction management with **@Transactional**, security with **@PreAuthorize**, caching with **@Cacheable**—these work seamlessly with interface-based dependencies.

Use it when building **layered architectures**: controllers depend on service interfaces, services depend on repository interfaces. Each layer defines the abstractions it needs. Don't create interfaces for **@RestController** classes—there's typically one implementation per endpoint. Don't create interfaces for simple **DTOs**, **domain entities**, or **configuration classes**. Those aren't dependencies that change.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Injecting concrete classes**: Freshers often inject the implementation directly—private final JpaUserRepository repository—instead of the interface. Even though Spring handles injection, this violates DIP because UserService now depends on a specific implementation.
- **Creating unnecessary interfaces**: Making an interface for every single class, including controllers and DTOs. Only create interfaces when there's a real abstraction need—multiple implementations or testing.
- **Field injection with @Autowired on concrete types**: Using @Autowired on private fields instead of constructor injection, and doing it on concrete classes instead of interfaces. This combines two anti-patterns: hidden dependencies and DIP violation.
- **Forgetting @Component family annotations**: If you implement an interface but forget @Repository or @Service on the implementation, Spring can't find it. The application fails at startup with a NoSuchBeanDefinitionException.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Interface injection**: inject the interface type in constructors, not the concrete implementation class—UserRepository not JpaUserRepository
**@Component annotations**: mark implementations with @Repository, @Service, or @Component so Spring can discover and instantiate them
**Constructor injection**: preferred over field injection because it makes dependencies explicit and enables testing without Spring
**Runtime resolution**: Spring resolves which implementation to inject at application startup based on classpath scanning
**@Primary and @Qualifier**: use these annotations when multiple implementations of an interface exist to tell Spring which one to inject
**High-level module owns interface**: the service layer defines the repository interface it needs—the repository module implements it
**No direct instantiation**: service classes never use new to create repositories—Spring handles all object creation and wiring

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Spring Boot makes it really easy to follow the Dependency Inversion Principle. Here's how it works. You start by defining an interface for what you need—let's say UserRepository. That interface declares methods like findById and save. Then you create a concrete implementation, maybe JpaUserRepository, and annotate it with @Repository. Spring sees that annotation and registers the class as a bean. Now in your service class, you inject the interface type, not the concrete class. So you write private final UserRepository userRepository in your constructor. Notice it's the interface, not JpaUserRepository. When Spring starts up, it scans for classes that implement UserRepository, finds JpaUserRepository, creates an instance, and injects it into your service. Your service class has no idea which implementation it gets. It only knows about the interface. That's DIP in action—the high-level service depends on an abstraction, and Spring provides the implementation. The benefit is decoupling. If I want to switch to a different database or add caching, I just create a new implementation of UserRepository. I don't touch UserService at all. In tests, I can inject a Mockito mock that implements UserRepository, and my tests run without a real database. A common mistake freshers make is injecting the concrete class—private final JpaUserRepository repository. Even though Spring still handles the injection, this violates DIP because now UserService depends on a specific implementation. If you change to a different repository, you have to change UserService code. Another mistake is using field injection with @Autowired. Constructor injection is better because it makes dependencies explicit and works without Spring in unit tests. The key thing to remember is that the service layer defines the interface it needs. The repository layer implements that interface. That's the inversion—the low-level module conforms to the high-level module's needs, not the other way around.

beats.content: When a class calls new on a concrete collaborator, it hardcodes that dependency. You can't swap it, you can't mock it in tests, and changing the collaborator often means changing the class too. That's tight coupling, and it's the DIP violation.

The fix is to receive the dependency through the constructor instead of creating it. The caller provides the concrete class. The class just knows the interface. Now you can pass in any implementation, including mocks in tests.

gotcha: not all new is a DIP violation. Using new for value objects like new ArrayList(), new BigDecimal(), or new LocalDate() is fine. Those are data containers with no substitution needed. The problem is new for services, repositories, or any class you'd want to swap or mock.

speakable_v2.cap: new inside a class is a DIP violation for services and repositories. For value objects it's fine. Inject collaborators, create values.

question: Why is new SomeClass() inside a class considered a DIP violation?
title: Using new inside a class violates DIP — tight coupling
direct_answer: Using new SomeClass inside a class creates a hard dependency on that specific implementation. The class cannot function without that exact concrete class, which is tight coupling. DIP says high-level modules shouldn't depend on specific low-level implementations—they should depend on abstractions. When you use new, you're tightly coupling to the concrete class and making the code untestable and inflexible.

sections.title: Why new Creates Tight Coupling
sections.content:
When you write **new SomeClass()** inside a method, you create a **compile-time dependency**. Your class cannot compile or run without that specific concrete class. This is **tight coupling**—the two classes are bound together. If SomeClass changes, your class might break. If SomeClass has dependencies, your class inherits them. If you want to test your class, you're forced to use the real SomeClass, even if it hits a database or calls an API. DIP says depend on **abstractions** like interfaces so you can swap implementations. Using new directly in code violates this because you're hardcoding a specific implementation.

Think of it like hardcoding a URL in code: new HTTPClient("https://api.example.com"). If the API changes, you have to recompile. But there's a critical distinction: using new for **value objects** like new ArrayList(), new BigDecimal("10.50"), or new User(id, name) is fine. Those aren't dependencies that change—they're data. The problem is new EmailService(), new MySQLRepository(), or new PaymentGateway()—those are **collaborators** your class depends on.

sections.title: DIP Violation with new Keyword
When new is Acceptable vs When It Violates DIP
sections.content: It's **fine to use new** for **value objects** and **data structures**: String, Integer, LocalDate, BigDecimal, ArrayList, HashMap, your own records and immutable entities like new Order(id, item). These represent data, not behavior dependencies. It's **fine to use new** for **exceptions**: throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid ID"). Exceptions aren't dependencies. It's a **DIP violation** to use new for **services, repositories, and infrastructure**: new EmailService(), new OrderRepository(), new HttpClient(), new KafkaProducer(). These are collaborators that your class depends on—they should be injected. It's a **DIP violation** to use new for **anything with side effects**: classes that access databases, call APIs, write files, send messages. If the class has external interactions, inject it instead of creating it.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking new is always bad**: Freshers sometimes avoid new entirely, even for value objects, and try to inject everything. You don't inject String or LocalDate—you create them with new or factory methods.
- **Creating dependencies inside methods**: Writing var repo = new SomeRepository() in each method instead of as a field. This is still tight coupling, just repeated multiple times.
- **Mixing new and injection**: Injecting some dependencies but creating others with new in the same class. Either inject all collaborators or you haven't decoupled.
- **Not recognizing the pattern**: If a class you're creating with new has its own dependencies (constructor parameters, calls to other services), that's a sign it should be injected, not created.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **new creates compile-time dependency**: using new SomeClass hardcodes a dependency on that specific concrete class
**Tight coupling**: the class cannot function without that exact implementation, making changes and testing difficult
**DIP violation**: high-level modules should depend on abstractions, not create concrete low-level implementations with new
**Value objects are fine**: using new for String, LocalDate, ArrayList, or your own data classes is not a DIP violation
**Collaborators must be injected**: services, repositories, and infrastructure classes should be injected, not created with new
**Testability**: when you use new for collaborators, you cannot replace them with mocks in tests—tests are forced to use real implementations
**Dependency creation vs object creation**: DIP is about dependency relationships, not all object creation—creating data objects is fine

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Using new inside a class creates a hard dependency on that specific concrete class. When you write new MySQLOrderRepository, your class is now tightly coupled to that exact implementation. It can't work without it. If you want to switch to Postgres, you have to change your code. If you want to test the class, you're stuck using the real MySQL repository, which means your test needs a running database. That's the problem. The Dependency Inversion Principle says your class should depend on abstractions, not concrete implementations. Instead of creating the repository with new, you should inject an OrderRepository interface through the constructor. Then Spring or your test can provide any implementation—MySQL in production, an in-memory version in tests, a mock in unit tests. Your class doesn't know and doesn't care which implementation it gets. Now here's an important distinction freshers often miss: not all uses of new are bad. It's perfectly fine to use new for value objects—things like new ArrayList, new BigDecimal, new LocalDate, or your own data classes like new Order. Those aren't dependencies. They're just data structures. The problem is using new for collaborators—other classes your code depends on for behavior, especially if those classes have side effects like database access, API calls, or file I/O. If a class talks to infrastructure, it should be injected, not created. The reason this matters for testing is straightforward. If OrderService creates its own repository with new, I can't replace it in a test. I'm forced to use the real repository, which is slow and brittle. But if the repository is injected, I can pass in a Mockito mock in my test. The test runs in milliseconds without any database. That's why DIP and dependency injection go hand in hand. DIP says depend on abstractions. Injection is how you provide those abstractions without using new.

sections.title: Understanding Dependency Inversion Principle
sections.content:
The Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP) is the **D** in SOLID. It flips traditional dependency flow: instead of high-level business logic depending on low-level implementation details like databases or file systems, both depend on **abstractions** (interfaces or abstract classes).

Think of it like a power outlet: your laptop doesn't depend on a specific power plant—it depends on the **outlet interface**. The power plant and your laptop both conform to that standard.

In Java, this means your **OrderService** shouldn't create or directly reference **MySQLOrderRepository**—instead, it depends on the **OrderRepository interface**. The concrete MySQL class implements that interface. This inverts the dependency direction: the low-level module now depends on (implements) the high-level module's interface. Without DIP, changes in low-level code force changes in high-level code. With DIP, you can swap implementations without touching business logic.

violet|Payoff|~swap implementations|DB, email, gateway interchangeable

sections.title: DIP in Action with Spring Boot
When to Apply DIP
sections.content:
Use DIP when your class collaborates with another class that has **infrastructure concerns**: database access, external APIs, file systems, email sending, payment gateways. If OrderService directly instantiated MySQLOrderRepository, switching to PostgreSQL would require changing OrderService code. With DIP, you just provide a different implementation of OrderRepository.

Apply DIP in **service layers** that contain business logic—they should depend on repository interfaces, not concrete DAOs.

Use it when you need **multiple implementations**: a real repository for production, an in-memory repository for tests, a caching repository for performance. Don't apply DIP to simple value objects like String, LocalDate, or your own immutable records—those are details, not dependencies that change.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing DIP with Dependency Injection**: DIP is a design principle about depending on abstractions. DI is a pattern for providing those dependencies. You can have DI without DIP (injecting concrete classes) and DIP without DI (manually passing interfaces). They work together but aren't the same.
- **Creating interfaces for every class**: Freshers sometimes make an interface for every single class, even DTOs or simple utilities. Only create interfaces when you need abstraction—when there are multiple implementations or when testing requires mocking.
- **Putting the interface in the wrong module**: The high-level module should own the interface it depends on. If OrderService needs OrderRepository, that interface lives in the service package, not the repository package. This is the inversion—low-level code conforms to high-level needs.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **High-level modules**: business logic classes like services shouldn't depend on low-level implementation details
**Abstractions**: both high-level and low-level modules depend on interfaces or abstract classes, not concrete classes
**Dependency direction**: DIP inverts the traditional flow where business logic depends on infrastructure—now infrastructure implements interfaces defined by business logic
**Decoupling**: changing database from MySQL to Postgres requires only a new implementation of the interface, not changes to business logic
**Testing**: DIP enables unit testing by allowing mock implementations to replace real dependencies
**Interface ownership**: the high-level module defines and owns the interface it depends on, following the Interface Segregation Principle
**Not everything needs abstraction**: value objects, DTOs, and domain entities don't need interfaces—only collaborators with changeable implementations do

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The Dependency Inversion Principle says high-level modules shouldn't depend on low-level modules—both should depend on abstractions. In a Spring Boot app, this means your service class depends on an interface like OrderRepository, not the concrete MySQLOrderRepository class. The principle inverts the traditional dependency flow. Normally, business logic depends on infrastructure code like database access. With DIP, you define an interface in your service layer that represents what you need. The infrastructure layer implements that interface. So the dependency points upward—the low-level module depends on the high-level module's interface. The key benefit is decoupling. If I want to switch from MySQL to Postgres, I just create a new PostgresOrderRepository that implements the same interface. My OrderService code doesn't change at all because it only knows about the interface. This also makes testing easy—I can inject a mock implementation in my unit tests without touching a real database. A common mistake freshers make is thinking DIP and Dependency Injection are the same thing. They're not. DIP is the principle about abstractions. DI is the pattern where you pass dependencies into a class instead of creating them with the new keyword. Spring's IoC container automates DI, which helps you follow DIP. But you could follow DIP without using Spring—you'd just have to wire things manually. The inversion part is important. It's not just about using interfaces. It's about who owns the interface. In traditional design, the low-level module defines the interface and the high-level module uses it. With DIP, the high-level module defines the interface it needs, and the low-level module implements it. That's the inversion—control flows from high to low.

question: What is the difference between Dependency Inversion Principle and Dependency Injection?
title: DIP vs Dependency Injection — principle vs pattern
direct_answer: DIP is a design principle that says depend on interfaces, not concrete classes. Dependency Injection is a pattern where a class receives its dependencies from outside instead of creating them internally. An IoC container like Spring automates DI by managing object creation and wiring. DIP is the goal; DI is the technique; IoC is the tool.

sections.title: DIP, DI, and IoC: Three Levels of Abstraction
sections.content:
These three concepts work together but operate at different levels. **DIP (Dependency Inversion Principle)** is a design principle—a guideline for structuring code. It says depend on abstractions, not concrete implementations. **DI (Dependency Injection)** is a design pattern—a specific technique for implementing DIP. Instead of a class creating its dependencies with new, the dependencies are passed in from outside (injected). **IoC (Inversion of Control) container** is a framework mechanism—Spring Boot's runtime system that automates DI. You annotate classes with @Service and @Repository, and Spring creates instances and injects them where needed.

Think of it like building a house: DIP is the architectural principle (rooms should connect via standard doorways). DI is the construction technique (use modular pre-built door frames). IoC is the construction company (Spring) that assembles everything according to your blueprints (configuration).

sections.title: When to Use Each Concept
sections.content:
Apply **DIP** whenever you design a class that collaborates with changeable dependencies—services, repositories, external APIs. Always depend on interfaces.

Use **DI pattern** to implement DIP: pass dependencies through constructors or setters instead of creating them with new. Constructor injection is the standard in Spring Boot.

Use **Spring's IoC container** when building production applications—it automates DI, manages singletons, handles lifecycle, and provides features like AOP and transaction management. For small utilities or standalone scripts, manual DI without a container works fine: just pass interfaces in constructors yourself. In unit tests, you use DI with mocking frameworks like Mockito—you inject mock implementations into the class under test. The IoC container isn't needed in tests; you wire dependencies manually.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Treating DIP and DI as synonyms**: Freshers often say DIP when they mean DI or vice versa. Remember: DIP is the why (depend on abstractions), DI is the how (inject from outside), IoC is the tool (Spring automates it).
- **Injecting concrete classes**: You can use DI without following DIP. If you inject MySQLOrderRepository directly instead of OrderRepository interface, you're using DI but violating DIP. The service still has a hard dependency on the concrete class.
- **Thinking IoC is required for DI**: You can do dependency injection manually in plain Java by passing dependencies through constructors. IoC containers like Spring just automate the wiring. In tests, you inject mocks manually without Spring.
- **Over-relying on field injection with @Autowired**: Constructor injection is preferred because it makes dependencies explicit and enables testing without reflection. Field injection hides dependencies and makes unit testing harder.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **DIP (Dependency Inversion Principle)**: design principle stating high-level modules should depend on abstractions, not concrete implementations
**DI (Dependency Injection)**: design pattern where dependencies are provided to a class from outside rather than created internally with new
**IoC (Inversion of Control)**: framework mechanism where Spring manages object creation and dependency wiring based on annotations and configuration
**Relationship**: DIP is the goal, DI is the implementation technique, IoC is the automation tool—they build on each other
**Constructor injection**: the preferred DI method in Spring Boot because it makes dependencies explicit and supports immutability
**Manual DI**: you can inject dependencies yourself without Spring—just pass interfaces through constructors in your code
**Testing**: unit tests use DI with mocks but typically don't use Spring's IoC container—you wire dependencies manually for speed

sections.title: Code Example
How to Answer
sections.content: These three terms are related but mean different things. The Dependency Inversion Principle is a design principle—the D in SOLID. It says your code should depend on abstractions like interfaces, not concrete classes. It's a guideline for how to structure your code. Dependency Injection is a design pattern that helps you follow DIP. Instead of a class creating its dependencies with the new keyword, the dependencies are passed in from outside—injected through the constructor or a setter. So if OrderService needs an OrderRepository, you don't write new MySQLOrderRepository inside OrderService. You pass the repository in through the constructor. That's dependency injection. Inversion of Control is a framework mechanism. Spring Boot's IoC container automates dependency injection. You annotate classes with @Service and @Repository, and Spring creates instances and wires them together at runtime. You don't manually call constructors—Spring does it for you based on your annotations. The relationship is this: DIP is the principle—the what and why. DI is the pattern—the how. IoC is the tool—Spring automating the how. You can use DI without Spring by manually passing dependencies in your code. You can even follow DIP without DI if you're very disciplined about always depending on interfaces, though that's harder. But in a Spring Boot app, you use all three together: you design with DIP by depending on interfaces, you implement it with DI by injecting dependencies, and Spring's IoC container handles the wiring automatically. A common mistake is thinking DIP and DI are the same thing. They're not. DIP is about abstractions—what you depend on. DI is about injection—where the dependency comes from. You can inject concrete classes, which uses DI but violates DIP.

question: How does DIP improve testability?
title: DIP and testability — injecting mocks via interfaces
direct_answer: DIP makes code testable by allowing you to inject mock implementations instead of real dependencies. If OrderService depends on the OrderRepository interface, your test can inject a Mockito mock that returns controlled data without hitting a database. If OrderService creates its own dependencies with new, you cannot replace them—tests are forced to use real infrastructure.

sections.title: How DIP Enables Effective Unit Testing
sections.content:
DIP is the foundation of **unit testing** in modern Java. When your class depends on an **interface** instead of a concrete class, you can **inject a mock** in tests.

A **mock** is a fake implementation that you control—it returns whatever data you want without real infrastructure. If OrderService depends on the OrderRepository interface, your test creates a Mockito mock of that interface and injects it. The mock returns test data instantly—no database, no network calls. If OrderService used **new MySQLOrderRepository()** internally, you cannot replace it. The test would need a real MySQL database running, connection configuration, test data setup—slow, brittle, and not a unit test anymore. DIP breaks this dependency at the **seam** (the interface boundary). Your test injects a different implementation of the same interface. The class under test doesn't know or care. This is why DIP is not optional in professional Java development—without it, you cannot write isolated, fast unit tests. Test-driven development (TDD) requires DIP because you write the test before the real implementation exists.

sections.title: Unit Testing with Mockito and DIP
When DIP's Testing Benefits Matter Most
sections.content:
DIP's testing advantage is critical for **unit testing services and business logic**. Service classes orchestrate operations across repositories, external APIs, message queues—each is a dependency that should be mocked. Without DIP, you'd need integration tests for every scenario, which are slow.

Use DIP testing benefits when testing **edge cases and error paths**: database failures, network timeouts, API errors. With mocks, you make the dependency throw an exception—when(repo.findById(1L)).thenThrow(new SQLException()). Testing this scenario with a real database is hard; with mocks it's one line.

Apply DIP when practicing **test-driven development (TDD)**: you write the test first, before the implementation exists. The test creates a mock of the interface. Later you implement the real class. Without DIP, TDD is impossible—you can't test what doesn't exist yet.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Mocking concrete classes**: Freshers sometimes try to mock the implementation class directly—Mockito.mock(MySQLOrderRepository.class). This is fragile because Mockito needs to create a proxy, and final methods can't be mocked. Always mock the interface.
- **Testing with real dependencies**: Writing unit tests that inject real Spring beans and hit a real database. That's an integration test, not a unit test. Unit tests inject mocks and run in isolation.
- **Not verifying interactions**: Using mocks but forgetting to verify that the class under test called the right methods—Mockito.verify(mockRepo).save(order). If you don't verify, you're not testing behavior.
- **Over-mocking**: Mocking value objects or simple classes that don't need it. You mock collaborators with side effects, not data classes.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Mock injection**: DIP allows you to inject Mockito mocks that implement the interface instead of real dependencies
**Isolation**: unit tests run in isolation without databases, APIs, or other infrastructure—mocks return controlled test data
**Speed**: tests with mocks execute in milliseconds because there's no I/O—tests with real dependencies take seconds
**Error testing**: mocks let you test error scenarios like database failures by making the mock throw exceptions
**Verify interactions**: use Mockito verify methods to confirm the class under test called the expected methods on dependencies
**TDD enablement**: test-driven development requires DIP because you write tests before implementations exist—mocks fill the gap
**Interface mocking**: always mock the interface type, not the concrete implementation class—interfaces are designed to be mocked

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: DIP makes code testable because it allows you to inject mock implementations instead of real ones. Here's how it works in practice. Let's say you have an OrderService that depends on OrderRepository. If OrderService follows DIP, it depends on the OrderRepository interface, and that interface is injected through the constructor. In production, Spring injects the real MySQLOrderRepository. But in a unit test, you inject a mock. You create the mock using Mockito—var mockRepo equals Mockito dot mock OrderRepository dot class. Then you tell the mock what to return: when mockRepo dot findById is called with ID one, return a test Order object. Now you create your OrderService and pass in the mock. When you call processOrder, the service uses your mock instead of a real database. The test runs instantly because there's no database, no network calls, nothing slow. It's a pure unit test. The key benefit is isolation. You're testing only the OrderService logic, not the database access code. If the test fails, you know the problem is in OrderService, not in the repository or database configuration. You can also test error scenarios easily. Let's say you want to test what happens when the database throws an exception. You just tell the mock to throw: when mockRepo dot findById then throw new SQLException. Now when you call processOrder, the service gets the exception and you can test that it handles it correctly. Testing this with a real database would be hard—you'd have to deliberately break the database somehow. With a mock, it's one line of code. This is why DIP is critical for test-driven development. In TDD, you write the test before the implementation. The test creates a mock of the interface. The interface defines what the service needs. Then you go write the real implementation later. Without DIP, you couldn't do this because you'd need the real implementation to exist before you could test. A common mistake freshers make is writing tests that use the real dependencies. They inject the actual Spring beans and let the test hit the database. That's an integration test, not a unit test. Integration tests are valuable but they're slow and test multiple components together. Unit tests with mocks are fast, isolated, and test one class at a time. Another mistake is forgetting to verify interactions. It's not enough to check that the method returns the right value. You also need to verify that it called save on the repository: Mockito dot verify mockRepo dot save. That's how you test behavior, not just output.
